title: Galois group
sentences: In Galois theory, a branch of abstract algebra, the Galois group of a certain type of field extension is a symmetry group characterizing how it extends the base field.
Each element of the Galois group is a transformation of the field extension which leaves each element of the base field fixed.

This connection between fields and groups, given by the fundamental theorem of Galois theory, allows for group-theoretic tools to be used on problems in field theory, such as describing the solutions to quintic polynomials.

The study of field extensions and their relationship to the polynomials that give rise to them via Galois groups is called Galois theory, so named in honor of Évariste Galois who first discovered them.

A field is a set, like the rational numbers Q or the real numbers R, on which the four operations of addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division are defined and have certain standardized properties.
Fields can be extended into larger fields with the same operations, such as how Q can be extended to R and R can be extended to the complex numbers C.

These extensions may arise when there is no solution to a given equation within the smaller field (the base field) but there is in the extension: for instance, x² = 2 has no solution in Q but has two solutions in its extension R.
The problem of identifying and classifying the extensions of a field can be made easier by using group theory.
Each extension of a field adds additional structure that is "invisible" to the base field, and the Galois group describes that structure.
It does this by considering transformations which change the extension but leave the base field unchanged.
For instance, the transformation of complex conjugation, which maps a + b i ↦ a − b i, leaves every real number fixed but generally does not leave complex numbers fixed.

The "Galois group of C over R", written Gal (C / R), is the cyclic group of order 2 (equivalently, the integers modulo 2), with its one non-identity element representing this transformation of complex conjugation.
Suppose that E is an extension of the field F (written as E / F and read "E over F").
An automorphism of E / F is defined to be an automorphism of E that fixes F pointwise.
In other words, an automorphism of E / F is an isomorphism α: E → E such that α (x) = x for each x ∈ F.
The set of all automorphisms of E / F forms a group with the operation of function composition.
This group is sometimes denoted by Aut (E / F).
If E / F is a Galois extension, then Aut (E / F) is called the Galois group of E / F, and is usually denoted by Gal (E / F).
If E / F is not a Galois extension, then the Galois group of E / F is sometimes defined as Aut (K / F), where K is the Galois closure of E.

Suppose K₁, K₂ are Galois extensions of k with Galois groups G₁, G₂.
The field K₁ K₂ with Galois group G = Gal (K₁ K₂ / k) has an injection G → G₁ × G₂ which is an isomorphism whenever K₁ ∩ K₂ = k.

The notation F(a) indicates the field extension obtained by adjoining an element a to the field F.
A useful tool for determining the Galois group of a polynomial comes from Eisenstein's criterion.

If a polynomial f ∈ F [ x ] factors into irreducible polynomials f = f₁ ⋯ fₖ the Galois group of f can be determined using the Galois groups of each fᵢ since the Galois group of f contains each of the Galois groups of the fᵢ.
Gal (F / F) is the trivial group that has a single element, namely the identity automorphism.
Another example of a Galois group which is trivial is Aut (R / Q).
Indeed, it can be shown that any automorphism of R must preserve the ordering of the real numbers and hence must be the identity.

The Galois group Gal (C / R) has two elements, the identity automorphism and the complex conjugation automorphism.
The degree two field extension Q (√2) / Q has the Galois group Gal (Q (√2) / Q) with two elements, the identity automorphism and the automorphism σ which exchanges √2 and − √2.
This example generalizes with 2 replaced by a prime number p ∈ N.
In fact, any finite abelian group can be found as the Galois group of some subfield of a cyclotomic field extension by the Kronecker–Weber theorem.
Another useful class of examples of Galois groups with finite abelian groups comes from finite fields.
If q is a prime power, and if F = F _q and E = F _qⁿ denote the Galois fields of order q and qⁿ respectively, then Gal (E / F) is cyclic of order n and generated by the Frobenius homomorphism.
The field extension Q (√2, √3) / Q is an example of a degree 4 field extension.
This has two automorphisms σ, τ where σ (√2) = −√2 and τ (√3) = −√3.
Since these two generators define a group of order 4, the Klein four-group, they determine the entire Galois group.
